query: Consider the following context: Melting properties are critical for designing novel materials, especially for discovering high-performance, high-melting refractory materials. Experimental measurements of these properties are extremely challenging due to their high melting temperatures. Complementary theoretical predictions are, therefore, indispensable. One of the most accurate approaches for this purpose is the ab initio free-energy approach based on density functional theory (DFT). However, it generally involves expensive thermodynamic integration using ab initio molecular dynamic simulations. The high computational cost makes high-throughput calculations infeasible. In that context, which method can be used for calculate its melting properties, including the melting temperature, entropy and enthalpy of fusion, and volume change at the melting point, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A two‐phase coexistence simulation approach that combines ab initio accuracy with machine‐learning interatomic potentials can be used to determine the melting temperature, entropy and enthalpy of fusion, and volume change at melting for refractory alloys with much lower computational cost than full ab initio thermodynamic integration.
generation.material_initial_state: A well‐ordered, crystalline refractory alloy (e.g., a refractory high‐entropy alloy) at ambient pressure.
generation.intervention: Replace expensive ab initio molecular dynamics thermodynamic integration with a two‐phase coexistence method using a machine‐learning potential trained on DFT data.
generation.conditions: Simulations conducted at high temperatures near the melting point and under ambient pressure; conditions that produce a solid–liquid interface in the simulation cell.
generation.structural_mediator: The coexistence interface between solid and liquid phases, whose structure and dynamics mediate the free energy balance at melting.
generation.mechanism: By simulating a cell containing both solid and liquid regions, the machine‐learning potential accurately reproduces DFT-level interatomic forces while permitting large-scale and long-timescale MD runs. Equilibration of the two phases yields the melting temperature and allows direct extraction of latent heat (and thus entropy of fusion) and volume changes, with lower computational expense than full ab initio thermodynamic integration.
generation.predicted_outcome: The method should predict melting temperatures, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, and volume changes within a reasonable margin (e.g., roughly within 10% error) of results obtained from full ab initio methods or experimental measurements, enabling higher-throughput screening of refractory systems.
generation.baseline: Traditional ab initio free-energy calculations via thermodynamic integration using DFT-based molecular dynamics, which are accurate but prohibitively expensive for high-throughput studies.
generation.boundary: The accuracy of the results will depend on the quality and transferability of the machine-learning potential; extreme anharmonicity near melting and differences in chemical complexity could limit the method’s precision.
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainty remains regarding the generalization of the trained ML potential to the full range of atomic motions near melting and its capability to capture subtle free energy differences in complex multi-component systems.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a refractory alloy sample and perform both simulation and experimental studies. In simulations, implement the two-phase coexistence method with a machine-learning potential trained on DFT data to compute the melting temperature, latent heat (from which entropy of fusion is derived), and volume change at the melting point. Parallel experimental measurements (e.g., differential scanning calorimetry, high-energy X-ray diffraction, and dilatometry) will be conducted under matching pressure conditions.
measurements: Melting temperature via in situ observation of phase coexistence (experimentally and in simulation)
Enthalpy of fusion from calorimetric measurements and simulation free-energy differences
Volume change at melting from dilatometry and simulation cell volume analysis
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the simulation predictions differ by more than an acceptable error margin (e.g., >10%) from the corresponding experimental measurements, then the hypothesis that the two-phase coexistence method with ML potentials can reliably capture melting properties is falsified.
